I came up with something like this idea when I was trying to figure
out a way to prevent people from directly benefiting from non-prey
ousts. This is the component of deal making that is lazy and
irritating. The goal was to take away the reward mechanism from the
game for these deals and have the deals naturally decrease while not
telling players what to do.

I am not sure that you can make a reasonable rule to just prevent
certain types of deal making. Player co-operation is one the
interesting components of the game, anyway.

For the record, I was a little reluctant to give zero vps for end
game. I don't want to have people get bored and transfer out. I think
players should be forced to 'earn' all vps they get. I leave you to
determine what I mean by 'earn'.

On 31 Jul 2003 02:04:47 -0700, wolflord wrote:

>Again, I believe that having problems with table deals is strongly
>dependent on

>1) personal reasons (previous experiences ) and belief (ideas ...

>2) the metagame you play in

>3) the people that make the deal...

>Apart from that, I don't believe it's a structural problem in this
>game, hence not a problem which needs a structural solution/change.

That's a lot that you're sweeping under the carpet. But a particular
structural problem concerns rush decks. If two of these sit next to
each other then the predator will typically do a table split deal
rather than trying to oust a prey who can fight back. Because the
rush decks are able to go across table so easily, their unholy
alliance then has a structural advantage over decks that are focussed
upon ousting their prey. The resulting dynamic is the antithesis of
what Garfield was trying to achieve. It's broken.

Andrew

A combat deck has, in almost all cases, the ability to rush any vampire
on the table. (If you were using Wynn or only Karsh, with no rush card
back up, that'd be different.) Being able to take down powerful
vampires can very easily change the balance of power on a table.

A vote deck very often packs Banishment and Kine Resources Contested,
historically. These can both be aimed around the table. Being able to
take out a vampire with Banishment can very easily change the balance of
power on a table - perhaps your predator was expecting to be able to use
it as a bouncer, and now it's five blood down in his uncontrolled
region. More recently, Baltimore Purge has the capacity to *SERIOUSLY*
rewrite the balance of power on a table. Similarly, Dramatic Upheaval
and Kindred Restructure don't just change the balance on the table -
they change the whole table. Parity Shift can move five pool from one
person to another, generating a ten pool swing.

Many decks include some form of bleed bounce. Remember, bleed bounce is
directable to anyone, in most of the obvious circumstances. (My Enemy's
Enemy is more predictable, but a poorer choice in many instances.) You
can throw that bleed for five at your prey, your grand-prey... *That*
can be a pretty big change. Suddenly he's taking a bleed for five from
nowhere.

Granted, most bleed decks don't get to throw their weight around willy
nilly - but !Malks and neoMalks get a good set of options there.

All of those can significantly alter the passage of a game and the
balance of a table. And all of them can be found in common archetypes.

I'm sure you can think of less common examples too - a well placed
Reality, Sensory Deprivation or Pentex Subversion?

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
On 1 Aug 2003, wolflord wrote:

> *Combat decks don't very often get the time/luxury to go rushing
> crosstable just in order to prevent a deal, since they're usually
> spending most of their time/actions/resources on either staying alive,
> or trying to build up to do something forward.

It's true, they don't very often have the luxury to do so. I think this
has more to do with combat decks generally being inadequate to the task at
hand. Peter Bakija struck upon a very important concept early on, which
is that a Rush deck must be able to out-act most of the decks on the
table. It took a while for that to sink through my personal aversion to
weenie decks, but I think if you can't multi-rush, or you aren't playing
a weenie deck to just get the actions outright, then your chances of
winning are very, very slim. Every other strategy has a reasonable chance
of winning with two or three minion actions a turn (more is obviously
better), because each of those actions have the capability to do, on
average, three pool to your prey. If one third of your actions succeed,
then your prey is taking a steady 3 pool/turn, and I believe that is a
sufficient benchmark for a successful strategy. By virtue of attacking
pool indirectly, rush decks need many more actions than this.

Combat decks built according to this standard could, in theory, be able to
afford to take table-balancing rush actions. However, another major
mis-application of otherwise sound strategy, when applied to a rush deck,
is the tearing whole hog for the maximum VP's you can get. Rush doesn't
work that way. IMO, one should take a very relaxed approach towards
anyone that is getting their first VP. It's only a problem when another
player is positioned to gain two that you may need to step out of the
normal predator-prey triangle. And in that case, you are likely to be
getting help from the rest of the table or at the least not arousing their
ire, as the target of your rush is clearly in a strong position to take
the game.

Apologies if this is in the "well, duh" category, but I thought I'd muse
out loud over my coffee this morning.

They often work well like that.

However, threads diverge in multiple different ways. Even if they
don't, a point that someone makes several posts into the thread will not
be the same point that was made in the first thread. Claiming that
someone is missing the point - because they're not addressing the claims
made in the first post when, uh, they were addressing claims in an
entirely different post - misses the point of the structure of the
medium. Many multiple conversations can occur at once. Complaining
that the conversation people are having over here doesn't address the
points made over there isn't terribly relevant.

Hence, follow-up in the right place, and address the points made in that
place. Here, the thread diverged from a "solution" regarding a
perceived problem with deal making into how you can attempt to cross-
table affect deals *now* and how/why some decks do or don't have the
capacity to do that. That's not missing the point of the first post,
that's thread drift.

vermil...@yahoo.com (vermillian) wrote in message news:<f987c6cd.03072...@posting.google.com>...
> Make withdrawing from the game worth zero VP, and being the last
> player alive worth zero VP as well. That way, the ONLY way you can
> score VP is to oust your prey.
>
> ~SV

What if we went incorporated an ELO scoring system into the current
ratings? :) I'm not really a major proponent of ELO, but using a
variation on this might provide both another incentives against
deal-making and for deal-breaking.

If each time a predator ousted their prey, the predator could also
earn a Win and the corresponding ELO ratings points from their prey.
This would create another disincentive for one player to "give away"
their own VP in a convoluted deal. As it stands now, it doesn't "hurt"
nearly as much to have your average VPs/game stat slightly decrease.

In this scenario, if a game went to time, the remaining predator-prey
pairs would be recorded as Ties. That would mean there would be one
more ELO pairing to calculate as opposed to a game that went to
completion (e.g. 4 ousts = 4 pairings, zero ousts = 5 pairings).

I will also echo Curevei's post and advocate prizes being awarded
partially at the game level. It doesn't have to be much--one booster
pack would probably do--but keeping players focused on the game at
hand is always a good thing.
